title: Unsecured Credentials: Private Keys
summary: This sub-technique is credential collection aimed at private cryptographic keys, which differs from the rest of the parent because the stolen object is an authentication factor in its own right rather than a text password. A private key proves identity for remote shell access, decrypts collected files, and signs authentication assertions, so theft survives password resets for every system that trusts the matching public key. The search is extension and directory driven, since keys live in predictable places and carry recognisable suffixes such as key, pem, pfx, p12 or the passphrase-protected private key of a mail encryption tool, and the secure shell directory in a user's home folder is the most common single target. On registered devices, keys that bind the device to a cloud identity service can be exported and used to impersonate the device. When a key is passphrase protected, the attacker still has options: capturing the passphrase as it is typed, or attacking the encrypted key offline. Detection combines file access auditing with the authentication side, where a key based logon from an unexpected host is the decisive signal.

beginner.definition: A private key is a long secret code that proves your identity to other computers. It is the file version of a password, and it is often more powerful. This sub-technique is when an attacker finds those key files and uses them to log in as you.
beginner.whyItMatters: Keys are often trusted by many servers at once, so one stolen key can open a large estate. They may not require a password at all. Even a key protected by a passphrase can be attacked, because the attacker has the file and unlimited time.
howItWorks: Administrators create key pairs, keeping one secret half on their own machine.
The secret half is stored in a file, often in a hidden folder in the home directory.
Key files use recognisable endings such as key, pem, pfx, or p12.
An attacker searches the disk for files with those endings and copies them.
They use the copied key to log in to servers instead of typing a password.
If a passphrase protects the key, they may watch you type it or attack it offline.
beginner.example: Think of a building where staff use a plastic badge instead of a spoken password. The badge is issued once and then accepted everywhere. If a visitor picks up a dropped badge, every reader in the building opens for them. Nothing was forced and no code was guessed. The badge simply proved an identity that was not theirs.
takeaways: Private keys are credentials, so store them encrypted and access controlled.
Protect the secure shell folder in each user's home directory.
Watch for key based logins from hosts that never used that key before.

objectives: Explain what a private key is and how it differs from a password.
Describe the file types and directories adversaries search for keys.
Explain why a passphrase protected key can still be compromised.
Explain how a device identity key enables impersonation of a device.
Identify the file access and authentication records that reveal key theft.
